**Mark Sutcliffe** (born July 14, 1968)[[1]](#cite_note-CBC-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Sutcliffe-2) is a Canadian politician who was elected the 59th [mayor of Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Ottawa "Mayor of Ottawa") in 2022[[3]](#cite_note-3) and reelected in 2026. Before entering politics, he hosted *Ottawa Today* on [1310News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIWW "CIWW") radio.

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mark_Sutcliffe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Mark Sutcliffe was born at the [Riverside Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Hospital "Ottawa Hospital") in Ottawa on July 14, 1968, the son of John Michael Sutcliffe and Florence Ng-Yelim.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[2]](#cite_note-Sutcliffe-2) Sutcliffe's maternal grandfather, Xavier, was born to a Chinese family in [Mauritius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritius "Mauritius") in 1902. Sutcliffe's maternal grandmother, Yolande, was French, and the two moved to [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"). The family moved to Canada during the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"). John Sutcliffe was also an immigrant, coming from [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire") in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). John and Florence met while working at the [Metropolitan Life Insurance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Life_Insurance_Company "Metropolitan Life Insurance Company").[[5]](#cite_note-Citizen-5)

Sutcliffe grew up in [McKellar Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKellar_Park "McKellar Park") in the city's west end. He graduated from [St. Pius X High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Pius_X_High_School_(Ottawa) "St. Pius X High School (Ottawa)"), and then studied political science[[5]](#cite_note-Citizen-5) at [Carleton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carleton_University "Carleton University") for one year before dropping out to take a job at radio station [CHEZ 106](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHEZ_106 "CHEZ 106").[[1]](#cite_note-CBC-1) At the same time, he started working as a news reader at [CFRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CFRA "CFRA"), and then became a news reporter for the *[Ottawa Business News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Business_News?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ottawa Business News (page does not exist)")*, and was the first play-by-play announcer for the [Ottawa Lynx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Lynx "Ottawa Lynx") baseball team. He then founded the *[Ottawa Business Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Business_Journal "Ottawa Business Journal")*, where he met his wife, Ginny.[[5]](#cite_note-Citizen-5)

## Political career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mark_Sutcliffe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Political career")]

Sutcliffe was elected [mayor of Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Ottawa "List of mayors of Ottawa") in the [2022 municipal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Ottawa_municipal_election "2022 Ottawa municipal election").[[6]](#cite_note-6) Described as a [centrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrism "Centrism"), Sutcliffe defeated [Catherine McKenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_McKenney "Catherine McKenney"), a progressive councillor supported by many [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party") and some [Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada") figures.[[7]](#cite_note-endorsements-7) Sutcliffe drew support from sitting Liberal and [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Conservative Party of Canada") politicians.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[7]](#cite_note-endorsements-7)

As mayor, Sutcliffe has emphasized affordability, housing, public safety, public transportation, and reducing government spending.[[9]](#cite_note-9) His council budgets have generally passed with wide margins, a shift from the more contentious dynamics of previous terms.[[10]](#cite_note-:0-10)[[11]](#cite_note-:1-11)[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12)[[13]](#cite_note-:3-13)

Sutcliffe’s first budget, in 2023, passed unanimously and kept property tax increases capped at 2.5% for 2023 and 2024, as he had pledged during the campaign. It also froze OC Transpo fares (though OC Transpo fares would increase in subsequent budgets), added $15 million to police funding, and increased funding for social service agencies.[[10]](#cite_note-:0-10) Subsequent budgets in 2025 and 2026 raised property taxes by 3.9% and 3.75%[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Sutcliffe introduced a housing plan aimed at speeding up approvals, lowering development costs and fees, and encouraging urban intensification and transit-oriented development.[[16]](#cite_note-16) In December 2025, Prime Minister [Mark Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Carney "Mark Carney") and Sutcliffe announced a $400 million federal-municipal agreement to build up to 3,000 homes in Ottawa, including more than 1,000 units through the city's affordable housing pipeline.[[17]](#cite_note-17) By April 2026, the city said this target had been surpassed, citing eight projects producing more than 1,100 affordable units.[[18]](#cite_note-18) That same month, council unanimously passed a Sutcliffe-introduced motion to double the rate of supportive housing construction.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

One major initiative started by [Jim Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Watson_(Canadian_politician) "Jim Watson (Canadian politician)") and continued under Sutcliffe has been Lansdowne 2.0, a redevelopment of the City-owned [Lansdowne Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lansdowne_Park "Lansdowne Park"). The project carries a total projected cost of $418.8 million, with the City claiming it's net share will be estimated at $130 million. It includes renovations to the north-side stands in [TD Place Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TD_Place_Stadium "TD Place Stadium"), reconstruction of the 57-year-old [TD Place Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TD_Place_Arena "TD Place Arena"), a new event centre adjacent to the stadium, and two residential towers. It also includes $14.4 million for affordable housing.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) The project has drawn objections from The [Ottawa Charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Charge "Ottawa Charge") of the [Professional Women's Hockey League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_Women's_Hockey_League "Professional Women's Hockey League"), which stated it would not play at the renovated arena if seating capacity is reduced from 8,585 to 5,500, opting instead to play at the [Canadian Tire Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Tire_Centre "Canadian Tire Centre") for the 2026–27 season.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

The 2024 budget passed 20–5 and maintained the 2.5% property tax cap. It allocated $214 million for housing, $140 million for road and bridge repairs, $13.4 million police funding increase, and further spending on infrastructure, sidewalks, parks, and community safety.[[11]](#cite_note-:1-11)
